subject: history
title: Mid-Tudor Crisis? Edward, Mary and Rebellion
welcome_lead: perspective on rebellion, religion and the 'crisis' decade.
meta_desc: -Level adventure on Edward VI's Protestantism 1547-53 and Mary I's Catholic restoration 1553-58.
final_note: You can debate whether mid-Tudor England really faced crisis.

concepts.def: Edward Seymour governed for the young Edward VI 1547-49, falling after the 1549 rebellions.
West Country rising against the new English liturgy; suppressed by Lord Russell after 4,000 deaths.
Norfolk agrarian rising under Robert Kett, defeated at Dussindale; 3,000 rebels killed.
John Dudley dominated 1550-53, deepening Protestant reform with the 1552 Prayer Book and Forty-Two Articles (1553).
January-February Kent rising against Mary's Spanish marriage; defeated outside London.
Burning of about 283 Protestants 1555-58, immortalised in Foxe's Acts and Monuments (1563).

walkthroughs.body_html: Edward succeeded as a minor in January 1547. Somerset's enclosure commissions, debasement and war with Scotland (Pinkie, September 1547) produced the 1549 rebellions. The 1549 Act of Uniformity imposed Cranmer's First Prayer Book. Somerset fell in October 1549; Northumberland (Dudley) consolidated by 1550 and drove sharper reform: the 1552 Prayer Book, Forty-Two Articles, dissolution of chantries.

Edward's 'Devise' attempted to bypass Mary in favour of Lady Jane Grey, who reigned nine days. Mary's coup succeeded with popular and noble support. The First Statute of Repeal (1553) and Second Statute (1554) returned England to papal obedience; Cardinal Pole arrived November 1554. The Marian burnings (1555-58) included Cranmer, Ridley and Latimer.

The 1554 Spanish marriage produced Wyatt's Rebellion. War alongside Philip cost Calais in January 1558. Yet Marian administrative reforms (the 1554 Privy Council overhaul, the 1558 Book of Rates) showed institutional resilience. Historians like Loach and Tittler reject the 'crisis' label, while Loades and Elton emphasise instability.

mcqs.q: How did Henry VII secure the Tudor dynasty after 1485?
options: Henry VII was universally popular because he ended the Wars of the Roses.
Through marriage to Elizabeth of York, ruthless control of the nobility (bonds and recognisances), financial discipline, and crushing Yorkist pretenders like Simnel and Warbeck.
William of Orange was Charles II's son and inherited the throne.
Henry VII was Richard III's nephew and inherited the throne legally.

mcqs.q: Why did Henry VIII break with Rome?
options: Because he wanted England to become Protestant.
Primarily for an annulment from Catherine of Aragon, but also to seize Church wealth and assert royal supremacy — not for Protestant theological reasons.
Because the Pope excommunicated him for marrying Anne Boleyn.
William of Orange was Charles II's son and inherited the throne.
